text: A film crew spent eighteen months in Chicago with a man at work: speeches, meetings, a breakfast program for children, the unglamorous labor of building a chapter. Fred Hampton led the Illinois Chapter of the Black Panther Party, and the footage exists because someone was recording while he was alive to be recorded. What Howard Alk assembled afterward has two halves that will not separate — the organizer in a room full of people, and the investigation into how the Chicago police killed him. The second half turns the first into evidence. Nothing is reconstructed. The camera was simply there, and then it was there again, in other rooms, asking other questions, an eighty-eight-minute record of a year and a half and of what ended it. The National Film Registry holds it.

The premise is a fidelity test, and the catch is that everyone involved acts for a living. Married less than a year, two celebrated performers are already wary of each other; he decides she is capable of infidelity, invents a Russian officer, puts on the uniform and the manner, and courts his own wife while she believes him out of town. Eighty-two minutes, mostly rooms. The comedy runs on a man committing hard to a role in front of the one person best equipped to catch him at it, and on the fact that he cannot win: if she resists, he has spent a week lying for nothing, and if she does not, he has arranged his own injury. Sidney Franklin directs it dry. The Academy gave the film a prize for acting, which is a joke the film had already made.

A man's own image steps out of him and starts coaching him on how to look innocent. Lee Gentry is a lawyer with a gift for argument and no fixed convictions: a young woman he is courting, a dancer he is discarding, a phrase ready for either. Ben Hecht, who made his living writing, directs, and seventy minutes is exactly the length of a story about a man talking himself into a corner at speed. The apparition is the strange part. Alibis get built on screen, out loud, with the guilty party consulting the half of himself that never objects. He does not agonize; he drafts. Watching a professional persuader turn the equipment on his own night, and hearing how quickly the excuses grow baroque, is the whole entertainment, and the film is not sentimental about him.

An emergency ward runs on talk: who asks what, who is on the other end of a telephone, which piece of paper has to arrive before a person can be treated. Frederick Wiseman filmed at Metropolitan Hospital in New York and gave eighty-four minutes to that traffic — intake, referral, waiting, the moment a decision is reached and the longer stretch before anyone acts on it. Skill is not the scarce thing here. Doctors know what they are doing; the resources, the procedures and the gaps between one department and the next arrive at the patient in the same instant, and the film keeps them in one frame. Cases pass through. Some are settled in minutes, some are handed on elsewhere, and the accumulation is a portrait of an institution spending itself on what comes through the door.

One line covers the plot: a frail boy wants the leader of a street gang to let him in. Frank Borzage takes seventy-four minutes over it, which is the tell — the film is about the machinery of that wanting, the ranks children invent, the trials they set each other, the seriousness with which a group of boys reproduces loyalty, rank and punishment among themselves. A body that cannot keep up becomes a moral problem in such a system. The child understands this before any adult explains it. Borzage plays none of it for charm; the smallness of the world is no reason to soften what happens inside it, and the result is a film about children in which the children are governed. The National Board of Review counted it among the year's ten best.

Charlie Banks looks for work the way other men go to a job — daily, on foot, and the hours pass either way. Billy Woodberry shot in Watts, and the subject is less unemployment than what unemployment does inside a house: to meals, to a marriage, to the small authority a man expects over his own afternoon. Eighty-five minutes, almost nothing raised in volume. Shots run long enough for a silence at the kitchen table to register as an argument, and long enough that errands, favors and half-days of casual labor start to look like a full week that pays nothing. Money is short; time is not. That arithmetic governs every scene, and no break in luck is offered to settle it. It sits now in the National Film Registry, a strange fate for a film so committed to the unremarkable.

Eleven minutes, 1910, and the story moves like a telegram: a child tells the chief that her father has killed her mother, riders go after him, and he is brought back to face the tribe's judgment. This is the era when a single reel had to plant a family, a crime and a pursuit before the film ran out, and the staging is accordingly frontal — action delivered to the camera, distances covered in one unbroken shot. What separates it from the period's usual Western traffic is where authority sits. The pursuit is the tribe's, the judgment is the tribe's, and the law being applied is its own. James Young Deer directed. The National Film Registry took the film in, under the title 1910 gave it, which no one would write today.

Eight years before Nanook of the North, a feature-length picture was made with a cast composed entirely of Native North Americans. Edward S. Curtis wrote and directed it in the Queen Charlotte Strait region of coastal British Columbia, with Kwakwaka'wakw performers, and the word to hold onto is fiction: a melodrama was written, and the world it moves through is the actual one of the people playing it. Those two jobs strain against each other for sixty-five minutes. A viewer gets neither ethnography nor pure invention but the friction — the material and ceremonial life of a community pressed into a plot shaped for 1914 ticket buyers. The National Film Registry keeps it, and it repays attention paid to the edges of the frame.

It begins by putting the audience on a roller coaster at Rockaways' Playland and lets the track make the case. The film exists to sell a projection system, and it is built like a sales call: a temple dance from Aida, Niagara Falls, a choir in Vienna, the canals of Venice, a military tattoo in Edinburgh, a bullfight, a camera riding in the nose of a low-flying B-25. Nothing links them except width. Sitting through a hundred and fifteen minutes of demonstration is a peculiar experience now, and an informative one: here is what 1952 believed would get people out of the house and into a theater. Merian C. Cooper directed. The Academy gave it a prize for its score, a decent clue as to how much of the sensation was carried by sound.

Almost the entire film stays in one suburban house, because that is where the poet stayed. Stevie Smith wrote lines with barbs in them and lived among housework, a London suburb and long conversations with her aunt; Robert Enders builds the picture out of that mismatch instead of explaining it away. A hundred and two minutes, mostly interiors, mostly speech. The pressure comes from how little room there is: religion, respectability and a man who would marry her all push in one direction, and refusing them takes daily effort rather than a single dramatic act. Wit is her instrument and also her cost. The National Board of Review placed it among the year's ten best, and the film's method is close to its subject's — small scale, precise, unwilling to be consoled.

Most people meet the Vietnam Memorial Wall years before they learn whose drawing it was. Freida Lee Mock spends eighty-three minutes on the person and the process — Maya Lin working, and the objects that result, from that wall to the Civil Rights Fountain Memorial. A monument is a strange thing to make: it is commissioned, debated, built by other hands, then handed over to strangers who use it however grief requires. A film about such work has to follow the object out of the studio, and this one does. What holds it together is temperament, the manner of someone who arrives at a decision and then explains it once, without pleading. It took the Academy Award for documentary feature, putting the deliberation in front of an audience that had only encountered finished surfaces.

Four minutes long, with no character, no story and nothing to read. Mary Ellen Bute set color against sound so that neither illustrates the other; shape, hue and tempo are treated as one material, cut and modulated together, held in a flux that is controlled rather than loose. A tarantella is a fast dance, and the film keeps that pulse. The pleasure is close to watching a musician play something difficult at speed — interest attaches to the control, since there is no subject to attach it to. This was 1940, and the piece runs about the length of a song. It sits now in the National Film Registry, filed among the features and the newsreels, and it is over before a viewer has finished settling into it.

Cameras were at Lakehurst, New Jersey for a routine item: a transatlantic airship easing in toward its mooring, the kind of arrival newsreels covered because the timetable could be trusted. Five minutes of film came back from that assignment, and it is not the film anyone was sent to shoot. What it caught took less than a minute. Since then the footage has been quoted so often, and in such fragments, that seeing it whole and in sequence is a different experience — the ordinary approach still in front of it, operators framing for a landing, a crowd standing where crowds stand. Hydrogen made the airship possible and made the business short-lived. The National Film Registry keeps the reel, shot by people whose job that day turned into something no one had a procedure for.

In 1946 an animation unit was given the job of explaining menstruation, and the result is ten minutes of diagrams. Jack Kinney directed. The interest now lies in the choices: what gets a cutaway and what gets a metaphor, how much anatomy could be put in front of a general audience, and the register settled on — plain, unhurried, instructional rather than cautionary. Drawing does particular work in a film like this, since a line can show an interior without showing a body, and a chart can be studied by a roomful of people who would not look at a photograph. It is also a record of what was considered sayable, and to whom. The National Film Registry keeps it, and the ten minutes are more revealing about 1946 than about anatomy.
